issues.failure_explanation: The general form space permits arbitrary shift indices in its vertical factors, whereas the asserted representation only contains the special cross-site factors $\dv u^\alpha_{-\mathbf1_i}\wedge\dv u^\beta_0$. For example, when $p=1$ and $q=2$, the vertically closed form $\dv u^1_0\wedge\dv u^2_0$ cannot equal a sum of terms involving the independent basis factors $\dv u^\alpha_{-1}\wedge\dv u^\beta_0$. Vertical closedness does not impose the claimed shift pattern.

issues.failure_explanation: The displayed reasoning establishes at most that every solution of the given system satisfies $\mcE^{\vartriangle}(\msL)=0$. It does not prove the converse implication, so the Euler--Lagrange equations may be strictly weaker and the claimed equivalence does not follow. Moreover, $\msL$ is initially obtained only through an equality restricted to the solution set, while an Euler--Lagrange operator requires a Lagrangian defined on an ambient prolongation space.

diagnostic_evidence.quote:
When the limit $\epsilon_\mbn^i\rightarrow 0$ is taken, $\Delta_{\mbn}^i$ tends to
$\upd\!x^i$ and
$\frac{\diffi }{\epsilon_\mbn^i}$ tends to the total
derivative  $D_i$.

issues.failure_explanation: A scalar edge length does not determine the coordinate covector $\upd x^i$ or the coordinate direction $D_i$ on a general mesh or manifold. Multiplying a fixed formal symbol by that length and then cancelling the length makes the resulting operator exactly the uniform index-lattice operator, independent of edge directions and mesh geometry. Thus the stated continuum limits and extension to arbitrary non-uniform meshes do not follow; they are valid at most for suitably aligned rectilinear product meshes with signed coordinate increments.

issues.failure_explanation: As displayed, exactness at $\Omega^{k,0}$ would require $\dv:\Omega^{k,0}\to\Omega^{k,1}$ to be injective because there is no incoming map. It is not: any nonzero horizontal $k$-form whose coefficients depend only on $\mbn$ is annihilated by $\dv$. The proof's homotopy is defined only for $l\geq1$ and establishes exactness only in positive vertical degrees.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: State exactness only at $\Omega^{k,l}$ for $l\geq1$, or augment the complex at degree zero by its subspace of vertically constant horizontal forms.
issues.overall_effect: The theorem overstates vertical exactness at degree zero, though the positive-degree exactness used to obtain vertical primitives can remain valid.
issues.title: The vertical complex is not exact at its displayed degree-zero term
issues.why_classification: A short local correction preserves the positive-degree result and the paper's uses of vertical primitives.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: As $\mcI^{\vartriangle}$ is a projection and the difference variational bicomplex is exact, a difference version of equality \eqref{eq:ii} holds.

issues.failure_explanation: Equation \eqref{eq:ii} concerns the differential operators $\mcI$ and $\upd_{\uph}$, not $\mcI^{\vartriangle}$ and $\dDh$, so it cannot establish the discrete endpoint identity. The body obtains the discrete analogue by assuming the very exactness under proof, making this dependency circular. In addition, the asserted homotopy identity is stated for $1\leq k\leq p$; at $k=p$ it would make every top horizontal form a divergence, contradicting the nonzero quotient measured by $\mcI^{\vartriangle}$. It can only have the unaugmented form in degrees below the top.
